contributions.headingText: Pure extragonadal teratomas consist of tissue components of the three germ cell layers and occur predominantly in neonates and infants. They arise along the migratory path of primordial germ cells.

Acceptable: teratoma, prepubertal type; germ cell tumour type I; congenital teratoma.
The sacrococcygeal area is the most common site, followed by the head and neck, CNS, and mediastinum {15613854; 2551691}.

Congenital teratoma manifests in utero, usually during the second trimester. Sonography reveals a solid or mixed cystic and solid mass {19122459}. Large lesions (> 100 mm) are associated with an increased risk of fetal demise and a high perinatal mortality {16952584}. Rapidly growing tumours can cause a vascular steal phenomenon with consecutive fetal hydrops, especially when the tumour is detected before the thirtieth week of gestation {2286911; 10701852; 15017565}.

Depending on their anatomical extension, sacrococcygeal teratomas (SCTs) can be classified into different types (see #20198Table 7.03). Type IV teratomas are diagnosed later in infancy than teratomas with external components and are frequently associated with yolk sac tumour (YST) foci {10614561; 9498381}.

In neonates, serum levels of AFP are physiologically elevated at least for the first 6–8 months of life {6163129; 9592840} and do not necessarily correlate with the presence of YST components {15613854}. After tumour resection, AFP levels usually decrease slowly but continuously {16621769}.

Extragonadal teratoma typically affects prepubertal patients {15613854; 2551691}. SCT constitutes 40–50% of extragonadal type I germ cell tumours and is one of the most common congenital tumours, with a reported incidence of 3.7–7.1 cases per 100 000 live births and an M:F ratio of 1:3–4 {22320869; 18973151; 9498381; 1403540; 23432104; 26454470}. Beyond the age of 6 months, the incidence of pure teratoma decreases, whereas the frequency of YST rises {14752882}. In postpubertal patients, pure teratoma is rare; in this age group teratomas are typically components of mixed germ cell tumours {14752882}.
SCTs are normally sporadic but can also be part of the autosomal dominant inherited Currarino triad (anorectal malformation, sacral agenesis, presacral mass) {6789651}.

The postulated cell of origin is a mismigrated primordial germ cell that escaped apoptosis {23417399; 17705807} and failed to maintain the primordial germ cell phenotype {31413324}. Extragonadal teratomas are diploid and do not harbour driver mutations {31413324; 17080330}. Whereas 12p alterations are a common feature of postpubertal type II germ cell tumour {12752258; 19288817}, extragonadal type I teratomas, especially SCT, lack chromosome 12p abnormalities {24051698; 30176765}.

Extragonadal teratomas vary in size but can reach > 15 mm {19417664; 15613854}. They are well demarcated, with a heterogeneous cut surface showing solid or cystic components containing fluid, debris, or hairy material. Congenital teratomas do not have a (pseudo)capsule, which can make complete resection difficult {17080330}.

Teratomas contain tissue of all three germ cell layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Immature tissue components like primitive neuroectodermal rosettes are a common feature of congenital SCT {15613854; 17080330}. Two grading systems for estimating the degree of immaturity have been proposed (see #20199Table 7.04), although the presence or degree of immaturity does not predict malignant behaviour in SCT {9737245; 10561269}. However, the frequency of admixed YST foci in teratoma rises with increasing grades of immaturity {9737245; 15613854}.

Essential: teratoma without other germ cell tumour components and without evidence of a gonadal primary.

Desirable: prepubertal age.
Pure extragonadal teratomas are benign and are not staged.

Pure extragonadal teratomas do not metastasize. In congenital teratomas, prognosis is dependent on size, structure (cystic better than solid), and the presence of hydrops fetalis {26114890}. In order to avoid local recurrence, complete resection (including coccygectomy in SCT) is mandatory {12721723; 10561269}. The degree of immaturity is not associated with malignant behaviour, which means that patients with immature teratoma do not benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy {18541896; 11283126; 10561269}. In SCT with malignant elements (e.g. YST), adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy is recommended, especially at a metastasized stage or after incomplete resection {11283126; 16735707; 11078494}.
